moves.spoken: Let's play one more blitz game. e4, c5, the knight to f3.
He's playing the Sicilian; we're going to play the Open Sicilian, which I've been doing.
He plays e5 — the Kalashnikov variation, a pretty common Sicilian; Black strikes in the centre immediately, but the drawbacks are pretty evident.
The drawbacks are that it weakens two squares, principally d6 and d5, and we have to manoeuvre our pieces to exploit them — so the knight to b5 is the main line here.

transposed into what's called the Sveshnikov. Now, what we don't want is for our knight to be easily dislodged from d5.
We want to keep this knight on d5, but what's preventing us is his knight on f6 — so we're going to develop our bishop to eliminate it.

I'm sort of trying to explain why the theory is theory. This knight on a3 everybody should notice is very misplaced — it has no prospects, so
what we're going to do is give this knight some prospects — manoeuvre it somewhere civilised — so we go c3 in order to deploy
this knight through c2; it's not ideal, but at least our knight is now doing something. This is the main line of the Sveshnikov; so far he's been playing all the theoretical moves, kudos to him.

Now, note that c4 is also a move here, but it would weaken the d4-square, though c4 is theoretical too. The other thing to notice is that there's a pawn on b5 sticking out like a sore thumb — how do we go about undermining or exploiting its weakness?

It's a very typical idea, you'll see it in the Ruy Lopez and many openings — we go a4 to break up this pawn and also deploy the rook via the a-file; it's always nice when a piece already participates without you having to move it.

He takes, and we'll take with the queen, and the queen ably performs the task previously fulfilled by the knight. Maybe I should have supported my knight by playing the knight to e3 — that's another way.
He's also given our bishop a very nice square — where can our bishop now go to support the knight?
We were waiting for the square to open up for the bishop — development is not something that should always be rushed; it's a priority, but make sure you're giving your pieces good squares first.

Now he's given up a pawn on a6 — I think we'll just snag that one; that's a free pawn in my book. There's a little pressure down the a-file to be careful of, particularly because this rook is unprotected, but

what I'm seeing is that I can later move my bishop back to b5, and that bishop will simultaneously defend the rook on a4 — so while it's something to keep an eye on, it's not something to be overly concerned about. He takes, we take; he could have taken with the rook, but I don't see a point in shying away from this tension, and even if he attacks the bishop again, we have many ways to defend it — we can defend it with our queen, dropping the queen back to lend additional support. He's good, not going down without a fight, but you can see the cracks beginning to show. Now is a great time to show why we deployed the knight to c2: there's a move I call a glue move — a move that glues together all the disparate parts of White's position; it stops the queen from attacking b2, lends further support to the bishop, and just glues everything together nicely. That's the knight to b4. Note that b2 was hanging — f2 isn't hanging, because it's protected by the king. Now we have time for simple prophylaxis: where's his knight going? To f4, obviously — how do we prevent it? By going g3. A good observation is that the d5-square is also free, but we don't want to rush a knight there, because the knight on b4 is fulfilling the crucial role of defending b2. He goes back, and now we complete our development by castling. He plays f5 — a lot of people would worry about him opening the file, but understand the drawback of pushing the f-pawn when castled: you weaken the diagonal, so this check on c4 might be very strong in a couple of moves. Let's take on f5, and if he takes back, we make a discovered check and his knight is lost. He can't recapture on f5 — well, he did, but this knight is defended by the rook, and that rook also defends the other rook, so it's overloaded, and by giving the check we expose the tension of the rooks. Boom and boom — we're up a knight and a pawn, and we're winning. The most important moment in the game was g3 — it frustrated him, he got impatient trying to create counterplay, and he fell apart very quickly. Let's capture the knight, and now, notice, the bishop and the queen can combine in a battery threatening checkmate, and his bishop on f6 is going to be lost as well, because to defend against it he has to give it up. He runs, we take; how do we keep harassing the king after it moves to f7? Notice the knight to d5 could be a fork. The bishop to c4 or the bishop to g6 are both good. Our goal is to get the king onto e7, a forkable square, so we assess all the checks we can make, including retreating moves — people often miss retreating moves, and they're the glue that makes an attack run. The bishop to g6 cuts the king off from f7; the queen to h3 forces the king onto e7, literally the only move, and that king walks right into the fork with the knight — we win the queen and the game. We didn't do anything extraordinary: we played the theoretical moves and he collapsed quite quickly.

I think we actually explained the game quite well, so no need to over-explain. The move c4 here, which some were suggesting, is also very fashionable theoretically, but the issue is that it weakens the d4-square, so it has a drawback; its strength is that you get your development out faster, because c4 comes with tempo, attacking the pawn on b5. I made a lot of knight moves in the early going — I did — but he also made a lot of concessions that allowed me to violate some of these rules; in particular, he weakened the d5-square. When you get to around 1500, you have to understand that the rules you follow in a very linear fashion as a beginner, you start to bend slowly — and one of them is that you can allow yourself to move the same piece more than once, because opening theory starts playing a role.
